label: Chapter 8
title: The Valley of the Shadow of Death

blocks.p: Then I saw in my dream that when Christian reached the borders of the Shadow of Death, he met two men, descendants of those who brought back a bad report of the good land [Num. 13], hurrying back the way they had come. Christian spoke to them.
“Where are you going?”
“Back! Back!” they said. “And we’d advise you to do the same, if you value either your life or your peace.”
“Why, what’s the matter?” said Christian.

“Matter!” they said. “We were going that way, just as you are, and we went as far as we dared. In fact we very nearly went too far to come back; for if we had gone a little farther, we wouldn’t be here to bring you the news.”
“But what did you run into?” said Christian.
“Why, we were nearly in the Valley of the Shadow of Death, but by good luck we looked ahead and saw the danger before we reached it.” [Ps. 44:19; 107:10]
“But what did you see?” said Christian.

“See! Why, the Valley itself, which is as dark as pitch. We saw goblins there, and satyrs, and dragons of the pit. We heard in that Valley a continual howling and yelling, like people in unspeakable misery, sitting there bound in affliction and chains. Over that Valley hang the discouraging clouds of confusion, and Death spreads his wings over it always. In a word, it is dreadful through and through, utterly without order.” [Job 3:5; 10:22]
“From what you’ve said,” said Christian, “I still don’t see anything to show that this isn’t my way to the harbor I long for.” [Jer. 2:6]
“Have it as your way, then. We won’t choose it for ours.”
So they parted, and Christian went on his way, but still with his sword drawn in his hand, in case he should be attacked.

Then I saw in my dream that, for as far as this valley stretched, there was a very deep ditch on the right-hand side. That is the ditch into which, in every age, the blind have led the blind, and both have perished there miserably. [Ps. 69:14-15] And on the left-hand side, there was a very dangerous bog, into which, if even a good man falls, he can find no bottom for his foot to stand on. King David once fell into that bog, and would no doubt have been smothered there, if the One who is able had not pulled him out.

The path here was also extremely narrow, and so good Christian was all the harder pressed. When he tried, in the dark, to avoid the ditch on one side, he was ready to tip over into the mud on the other; and when he tried to escape the mud, he would have fallen into the ditch without the greatest care. So he went on, and I heard him sigh bitterly here; for besides the dangers I have described, the path was so dark that often, when he lifted his foot to step forward, he did not know where or on what he would set it down next.

v: Poor man! Where are you now? Your day is night.
Good man, don’t be cast down: your course is right.
Your road to heaven runs past the gates of hell;
cheer up, hold on, with you it will go well.

blocks.p: About the middle of this valley, I saw that the mouth of hell was there, and it stood right beside the road. Now, thought Christian, what shall I do? Every so often the flame and smoke would pour out in such quantities, with sparks and hideous noises (things that cared nothing for Christian’s sword, as Apollyon had), that he was forced to put his sword away and take up another weapon, called All-Prayer. [Eph. 6:18] So I heard him cry out, “O Lord, I beg you, save my soul!” [Ps. 116:4]

He went on like this for a long while, and still the flames kept reaching toward him. He heard mournful voices, too, and rushing back and forth, so that sometimes he thought he would be torn to pieces, or trampled down like mud in the streets. He saw this frightful sight and heard these dreadful noises for several miles together. Then, coming to a place where he thought he heard a company of fiends coming forward to meet him, he stopped and began to think what he had better do. Sometimes he half thought of going back. Then again he thought he might be halfway through the valley. He remembered, too, how many dangers he had already overcome, and that the danger of going back might be much greater than the danger of going forward. So he resolved to go on.

Yet the fiends seemed to come nearer and nearer; but when they had come almost up to him, he cried out with the most passionate voice, “I will walk in the strength of the Lord God!” And they fell back, and came no farther.

There is one thing I must not leave out. I noticed that by now poor Christian was so bewildered that he did not know his own voice; and this is how I saw it. Just as he came opposite the mouth of the burning pit, one of the wicked ones got behind him, stepped up softly, and whispered many terrible blasphemies to him, which he truly believed had come from his own mind. This tried Christian more than anything he had met before: to think that he should now blaspheme the One he had loved so much. Yet if he could have helped it, he would never have done it; but he did not have the presence of mind either to stop his ears or to realize where these blasphemies came from.

When Christian had traveled in this miserable state for a good while, he thought he heard the voice of a man somewhere ahead of him, saying, “Though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me.” [Ps. 23:4]
Then he was glad, and for these reasons.
First, because he gathered from it that some who feared God were in this valley as well as he.

Second, because he saw that God was with them, even in that dark and dismal place. And why not with me? he thought, even though, because of what hinders sight in this place, I cannot perceive it. [Job 9:11]
Third, because he hoped that if he could catch up with them, he would soon have company.

So he went on, and called out to the one ahead of him; but that one did not know what to answer, because he too thought he was alone. And by and by the day broke. Then Christian said, “He has turned ‘the shadow of death into morning.’” [Amos 5:8]

Now, with morning come, he looked back, not because he wanted to return, but to see by daylight what dangers he had passed through in the dark. He saw more clearly the ditch on the one side and the mud on the other, and how narrow the path was that ran between them. He saw the goblins, satyrs, and dragons of the pit now, too, but all far off (for after daybreak they did not come near). Yet they were revealed to him, as it is written: “He reveals the deep things of darkness and brings utter darkness into the light.” [Job 12:22]

Now Christian was deeply moved by his deliverance from all the dangers of his lonely road. He had feared them more before, but he saw them more clearly now, because the light of day made them plain. And about this time the sun was rising, which was another mercy to Christian. For you must understand that, though the first part of the Valley of the Shadow of Death was dangerous, the second part, which he still had to go through, was, if possible, far more dangerous. From the place where he now stood to the very end of the valley, the way was so full of snares, traps, springes, and nets on this side, and so full of pits, pitfalls, deep holes, and sudden drops on that side, that if it had been dark now, as it was when he came through the first part, then even if he had had a thousand souls, he would by all reason have lost them all. But, as I just said, the sun was rising.
Then he said, “His lamp shines on my head, and by his light I walk through darkness.” [Job 29:3]

In this light, then, he came to the end of the valley. Now I saw in my dream that at the end of this valley lay blood, bones, ashes, and the mangled bodies of men, of pilgrims who had come this way before. While I was wondering what the reason could be, I saw a little ahead of me a cave where two giants, Pope and Pagan, lived in former times. It was by their power and tyranny that the men whose bones, blood, and ashes lay there had been cruelly put to death.

But Christian went past this place without much danger, which surprised me somewhat. I have since learned, though, that Pagan has been dead a long time; and as for the other, though he is still alive, he has grown so feeble with age, and so stiff in his joints from the many hard knocks he took in his younger days, that now he can do little more than sit in the mouth of his cave, grinning at pilgrims as they go by, and biting his nails because he cannot get at them.
